extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in philosophy/history/methodology of mathematics (mathematicians, students, philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: A review/excerpt and extended summary of Imre Lakatos's Proofs and Refutations, extracting the methodological criteria, terminology, and patterns Lakatos uses to describe how mathematical knowledge develops through conjectures, proofs, and refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of mathematical discovery (4 stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Primitive conjecture. (2) Proof (a rough thought-experiment or argument, decomposing the primitive conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas). (3) Global counterexamples emerge. (4) Proof re-examined: the 'guilty lemma' is spotted and built into the conjecture as a condition; the improved conjecture (proof-generated concept) supersedes the primitive conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos presents this as the simple pattern by which informal mathematical theories grow; he notes the steps are not infallible and the order can sometimes vary (step 4 may precede step 3). The subsequent process includes further examination and turning counterexamples into examples for new theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between local counterexamples (which refute a hidden lemma inside a proof) and global counterexamples (which directly refute the primitive conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos repeatedly uses this distinction (e.g., Seidel's analysis of Cauchy's proof) to locate the 'guilty lemma' in a proof-analysis and to motivate reformulation of conjectures and introduction of new conditions (such as uniform convergence vs pointwise convergence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminating a counterexample by ad hoc redefinition of terms so that the counterexample no longer counts as a counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reinterpreting 'polyhedron' so that previously counterexample objects are declared outside the class; Lakatos calls this 'monster-barring' and notes it can hide essential changes in meaning behind identical linguistic expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring (domain exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defending a conjecture by introducing an extraneous condition that excludes the counterexample (e.g., restricting to convex polyhedra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos contrasts this with lemma-incorporation: exception-barring adds conditions external to the argument rather than deriving them from the proof itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piecemeal exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing counterexamples or problematic cases by excluding them piece by piece from the domain of the conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the recurrent methods used historically when confronting counterexamples; often leads to narrower, less explanatory theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawing a conjecture or claim strategically in response to criticism or counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as one of the responses mathematicians use during the heuristic/progressive process of proofs and refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma-incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Making an implicit or 'guilty' lemma explicit and incorporating it into the statement of the theorem; the improved theorem 'sums up' the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos describes the lemma-incorporating method as relying solely on the argument and producing the lemma-incorporating theorem: e.g., 'All simple polyhedra with simply-connected faces are Eulerian.' This is presented as a non-ad hoc improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-generated theorem / proof-generated concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem or concept that arises from making explicit the assumptions or lemmas revealed by proof-analysis; the proof itself generates the improved conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos emphasizes that often the new condition in an improved conjecture is discovered by analyzing the original proof's hidden hypotheses rather than imposed arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-stretching
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the scope/definition of a concept to cover novel or 'alien' objects, thereby producing refutations which reveal conceptual inadequacy and motivate new conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos gives examples where refutationists stretch concepts to include ring-shaped faces or non-simple polyhedra; concept-stretching explains why some historical refutations appeared absurd to contemporaries who had a narrower concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as thought-experiment / quasi-experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Lakatos proposes retaining 'proof' as a thought-experiment that decomposes a conjecture into subconjectures/lemmas and embeds it in wider bodies of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher-character in the dialogues treats proofs as heuristics useful even if they fail to accomplish their intended task; proofs can lead to discoveries even when they don't establish final truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs do not (finally) establish truth; avoid 'QED' closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Lakatos argues 'one does not prove what one has set out to prove. Therefore no proof should conclude with the words: "Quod erat demonstrandum".' Proofs are parts of an ongoing, fallible process rather than final certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He points to infinite regress in proofs and suggests proving is a game; certainty is never achieved and foundations are never found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutations are conclusive; proofs are psychological
rubrics_metrics.description: Refutations (counterexamples) are conclusive in undermining claims, while proofs have a psychological element (they convince but may not be final).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos explicitly states 'Only refutations are conclusive — proofs are a matter of psychology.' This privileges counterexamples in methodological weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose and remove implicit lemmas / hidden assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify implicit lemmas assumed by a proof (e.g., Cauchy's assumption of familiarity with the theory of real numbers) and make them explicit to avoid misleading claims of rigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos criticizes authors who 'assume familiarity with lemmas of type x' and praises the move toward collecting background lemmas explicitly in textbooks (Weierstrass, Landau) to increase rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing criteria of rigor reorganize mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in what counts as 'rigorous proof' (e.g., arithmetical vs geometrical intuition, Weierstrassian rigour) lead to major reorganizations of mathematical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos traces historical changes (Pythagoreans, 18th/19th century debates, set-theoretical disputes) to show how revisions in rigour redefine acceptable proofs and restructure disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and taste as acceptance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptability of proofs/theories rises with elegance; 'mathematical taste' plays an important (though mysterious) role in scientific advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes and discussion (e.g., von Neumann on 'well-developed taste') underscore that elegance and aesthetic judgments influence which proofs are preferred and accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for mathematical taste and critics to prevent trivialities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical taste and critical scrutiny are necessary to stem 'pretentious trivialities' and shallow generalizations in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos (via Polya) warns about fashionable shallow generalizations; taste and critical reviewers help maintain depth and relevance in mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMEGA criterion: certainty and finality (sufficiency and necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable theorem should be both certain (no counterexamples within its domain) and final (no examples outside its domain); ideally, conditions should be both sufficient and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos frames a methodological desire for theorems that draw a clear dividing line between examples and counterexamples, not merely restrict to a safe domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and concept-formation: choose terms to maximize applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the 'right language' (terminology and conceptual framework) can allow proofs to apply to many objects without change; good concept-formation broadens applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré quote: 'Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.' Lakatos urges attention to how language changes as knowledge grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretational caution: narrow vs wide readings alter truth-values
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition admits a sufficiently narrow interpretation making it true and a sufficiently wide one making it false; one must be explicit about intended interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos labels the narrow reading as dogmatist/verificationist and the wide reading as sceptical/refutationist; this affects how we judge theorems and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of observation / quasi-empirical methods in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and quasi-experimental methods (e.g., mineralogical collections leading to cube-in-cube counterexamples) are important stimuli in mathematical discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos gives historical examples where empirical-like observations inspired counterexamples and new conjectures, challenging strict formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counterexamples to drive theory improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples are productive: they reveal hidden assumptions, motivate lemma-incorporation, concept refinement, or new fields of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the book Lakatos shows how successive counterexamples lead to refined conjectures and expanded theory rather than merely defeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of convergence in analysis: uniform vs pointwise
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish pointwise from uniform convergence: uniform convergence is the stronger condition needed to secure continuity of the limit of continuous functions (Seidel's correction of Cauchy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a case study (Cauchy's conjecture) illustrating how identifying the correct hypothesis (uniform convergence) resolves counterexamples and refines proofs.
